Assessment:
- 29-year-old female with several months of facial lesions; exam documents 3 discrete atrophic blue-tinged plaques on forehead and bilateral cheeks. Punch biopsy (H&E) and DIF reported as normal. Multiple historical and symptomatic details are not recalled by the patient and are therefore undocumented.

Plan:
- Diagnostic procedures completed: punch biopsy with H&E and DIF (both normal).
- Additional history elements remain to be obtained (menstrual history, topical steroid use, symptomatology, effect of sun, presence of scale/plugging) per the clinical record.

[THOUGHT] 
This 29-year-old woman has several months of stable facial lesions consisting of three discrete, atrophic, blue-tinged plaques on the forehead and bilateral cheeks. The location (central face), chronicity (months), and appearance (atrophic, violaceous/blue-tinged plaques) most strongly suggest a chronic cutaneous process rather than acneiform disease, infection, or simple postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Leading diagnostic considerations include chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid lupus), localized scleroderma (morphea), cutaneous sarcoidosis, and pigmentary disorders (e.g., ashy dermatosis or nevus of Ota). 

Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) classically produces well-demarcated, erythematous-to-violaceous plaques on the face with follicular plugging and eventual atrophy/scarring; it commonly affects women of this age group and can be mistaken for acne or other facial dermatoses. Although punch biopsy (H&E) and DIF were reported as normal, sampling error (biopsy from a burnt-out or central area rather than the active margin) can yield nondiagnostic results; DIF may be negative in a minority of cases. Morphea often produces indurated sclerotic plaques with a lilac ring, and sarcoidosis would show granulomas on histology, neither of which are supported by the (albeit normal) biopsy or the clinical distribution as strongly as DLE. Pigmentary disorders typically lack true atrophy. 

Given the clinical pattern—atrophic, violaceous/blue-tinged facial plaques in a young woman—the single most likely diagnosis is chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid lupus erythematosus), recognizing that nondiagnostic biopsy results do not exclude the condition and repeat or deeper biopsy/clinicopathologic correlation (including photosensitivity history, scale/follicular plugging on exam, serologies, and repeat DIF targeted to active margin) is warranted to confirm the diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS]
Discoid lupus erythematosus (chronic cutaneous lupus)

[THOUGHT] 
The proposed diagnosis of discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is not supported by the available data. Key clinical features of DLE (well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques with adherent scale/follicular plugging, photosensitivity, progression to scarring/atrophy) are undocumented or explicitly unknown. Critically, the punch biopsy (H&E) and DIF — the diagnostic studies most likely to show interface dermatitis, basement membrane thickening/mucin, and granular Ig/C3 deposition in DLE — are reported as normal. A normal H&E and normal DIF strongly argue against DLE unless the biopsy sampling or processing was inadequate. There is no photographic documentation or detailed lesion description (scale, induration, pigment changes) and many relevant history items (topical steroid use, evolution, photosensitivity, symptoms) are missing.

Red flags / critical missing items:
- Normal H&E and DIF: major red flag against DLE; requires re-evaluation of pathology or repeat biopsy.
- Lack of documentation of classic DLE findings (adherent scale/follicular plugging, scarring, photosensitivity).
- No clinical photographs or dermoscopy to corroborate lesion appearance.
- No information about possible topical steroid use (can alter morphology).
- No special stains/review of pathology for mucin, sclerosis, or other entities.

Given these gaps, the diagnosis is not sufficiently established.

[DECISION] INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK] 
To support or refute DLE (or establish an alternative diagnosis) obtain the following specific items:

1. Detailed clinical information:
   - High-quality clinical photographs of all lesions (multiple views; include scale/close-up).
   - Precise lesion description: presence/absence of adherent scale, follicular plugging, induration versus atrophy, color (erythematous vs blue-tinged vs violaceous), evolution over time, presence of scarring or pigment change.
   - Symptoms: pain, tenderness, pruritus, photosensitivity (worsening after sun exposure), timing/course.
   - Complete topical/systemic medication history including any prior or current topical corticosteroids, duration and potency.
   - Full skin exam documentation beyond the three plaques (scalp, ears, mucosa).

2. Pathology review and possible repeat biopsy:
   - Have the existing slides reviewed by a dermatopathologist with correlation to clinical photos.
   - If still nondiagnostic and clinical suspicion persists, repeat biopsy (preferably an incisional/punch including active edge and deeper dermis/subcutis). Request serial sections.
   - Request special stains as indicated: PAS (fungal), Alcian blue (mucin), Masson trichrome (sclerosis), and immunostaining if needed.
   - If DLE remains suspected, confirm DIF on an appropriate perilesional specimen (if prior DIF was not perilesional).

3. Adjunctive testing to broaden differential:
   - Consider ANA and other connective tissue serologies if systemic lupus is a concern.
   - Consider KOH prep/ fungal culture or Wood's lamp if tinea or pigmentary/fungal causes are possible.
   - Consider dermoscopy to look for follicular plugging or features of other dermatoses.
   - Consider evaluation for morphea/localized scleroderma if induration/sclerosis suspected.

Collecting the above will allow a conclusive determination for or against discoid lupus and identification of alternative diagnoses.

Diagnostician:

[THOUGHT] 
This 29-year-old woman has several months of stable facial lesions consisting of three discrete, atrophic, blue-tinged plaques on the forehead and bilateral cheeks. The location (central face), chronicity (months), and appearance (atrophic, violaceous/blue-tinged plaques) most strongly suggest a chronic cutaneous process rather than acneiform disease, infection, or simple postinflammatory hyperpigmentation. Leading diagnostic considerations include chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid lupus), localized scleroderma (morphea), cutaneous sarcoidosis, and pigmentary disorders (e.g., ashy dermatosis or nevus of Ota). 

Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) classically produces well-demarcated, erythematous-to-violaceous plaques on the face with follicular plugging and eventual atrophy/scarring; it commonly affects women of this age group and can be mistaken for acne or other facial dermatoses. Although punch biopsy (H&E) and DIF were reported as normal, sampling error (biopsy from a burnt-out or central area rather than the active margin) can yield nondiagnostic results; DIF may be negative in a minority of cases. Morphea often produces indurated sclerotic plaques with a lilac ring, and sarcoidosis would show granulomas on histology, neither of which are supported by the (albeit normal) biopsy or the clinical distribution as strongly as DLE. Pigmentary disorders typically lack true atrophy.

Discoid lupus erythematosus (chronic cutaneous lupus)

ANALYSIS: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1–L3 and typically presents with transient genital lesion followed by painful inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy (buboes) and sometimes proctocolitis. Primary genital HSV presents with grouped painful vesicles/ulcers and can cause tender regional lymphadenopathy but has a different etiology, lesion morphology, course, and diagnostic testing (HSV PCR vs NAAT for C. trachomatis). These are distinct diagnoses.

VERDICT: INCORRECT

ANALYSIS: Corticosteroid-induced atrophy is skin thinning, telangiectasia, and loss of subcutaneous tissue after chronic steroid use. Discoid lupus erythematosus (chronic cutaneous lupus) produces scaly, erythematous discoid plaques with follicular plugging, scarring and potential alopecia and has a different pathogenesis and histopathology. Though both can produce atrophic changes, they are not clinically equivalent.

VERDICT: INCORRECT
